1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I was among the exiles by the Chebar canal, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.<sup>2</sup>On the fifth day of the month (it was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin),<sup>3</sup>the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the Chebar canal, and the hand of the LORD was upon him there.<sup>4</sup>As I looked, behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually, and in the midst of the fire, as it were gleaming metal.<sup>5</sup>And from the midst of it came the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance: they had a human likeness,<sup>6</sup>but each had four faces, and each of them had four wings.<sup>7</sup>Their legs were straight, and the soles of their feet were like the sole of a calf's foot. And they sparkled like burnished bronze.<sup>8</sup>Under their wings on their four sides they had human hands. And the four had their faces and their wings thus:<sup>9</sup>their wings touched one another. Each one of them went straight forward, without turning as they went.<sup>10</sup>As for the likeness of their faces, each had a human face. The four had the face of a lion on the right side, the four had the face of an ox on the left side, and the four had the face of an eagle.<sup>11</sup>Such were their faces. And their wings were spread out above. Each creature had two wings, each of which touched the wing of another, while two covered their bodies.<sup>12</sup>And each went straight forward. Wherever the spirit would go, they went, without turning as they went.<sup>13</sup>As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of torches moving to and fro among the living creatures. And the fire was bright, and out of the fire went forth lightning.<sup>14</sup>And the living creatures darted to and fro, like the appearance of a flash of lightning.<sup>15</sup>Now as I looked at the living creatures, I saw a wheel on the earth beside the living creatures, one for each of the four of them.<sup>16</sup>As for the appearance of the wheels and their construction: their appearance was like the gleaming of beryl. And the four had the same likeness, their appearance and construction being as it were a wheel within a wheel.<sup>17</sup>When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went.<sup>18</sup>And their rims were tall and awesome, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.<sup>19</sup>And when the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them; and when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose.<sup>20</sup>Wherever the spirit wanted to go, they went, and the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.<sup>21</sup>When those went, these went; and when those stood, these stood; and when those rose from the earth, the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.<sup>22</sup>Over the heads of the living creatures there was the likeness of an expanse, shining like awe-inspiring crystal, spread out above their heads.<sup>23</sup>And under the expanse their wings were stretched out straight, one toward another. And each creature had two wings covering its body.<sup>24</sup>And when they went, I heard the sound of their wings like the sound of many waters, like the sound of the Almighty, a sound of tumult like the sound of an army. When they stood still, they let down their wings.<sup>25</sup>And there came a voice from above the expanse over their heads. When they stood still, they let down their wings.<sup>26</sup>And above the expanse over their heads there was the likeness of a throne, in appearance like sapphire; and seated above the likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance.<sup>27</sup>And upward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were gleaming metal, like the appearance of fire enclosed all around. And downward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and there was brightness around him.<sup>28</sup>Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel begins with a date and a place: In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I was among the exiles by the Chebar canal, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God (v. 1). It was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin (v. 2). A priest far from the temple was sitting by a canal in Babylon, and there the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel the priest, and the hand of the LORD was upon him there (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The God of Israel is not confined to Jerusalem; he opens heaven over his people in exile.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I was among the exiles by the Chebar canal, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God. On the fifth day of the month (it was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin), the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the Chebar canal, and the hand of the LORD was upon him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I was among the exiles by the Chebar canal, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.

Picture where Ezekiel is. Not in the temple courts in Jerusalem, but hundreds of miles away in Babylon, sitting beside an irrigation canal with a settlement of deported Judeans. Five years earlier the Babylonians had emptied Jerusalem of its king, its officials, its soldiers and its skilled workers (2 Kgs 24:14-15), and Ezekiel was among them.

In the thirtieth year is not explained. Most likely it is Ezekiel's own age. That would make it a painful birthday: thirty was the age at which a priest began to do the work in the tent of meeting (Num 4:3). The year he should have started serving at the altar, he was a refugee by a canal with no temple within reach.

And exactly there, the heavens were opened. God did not wait for Ezekiel to get back to the holy city. He came to the place of exile. The ESV notes that visions of God may also be rendered "visions from God" — they are both. God gave the visions, and God is what Ezekiel saw.

That is the first word of this book to anyone who feels far from where God is supposed to be — in a hospital, a prison, a foreign country, a season of spiritual dryness. Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (Ps 139:7). The heavens can open over a canal in Babylon.

On the fifth day of the month (it was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin),

The exiles counted time from the day their king was taken. It is 593 BC. Jerusalem is still standing, and many of the exiles expect to go home soon. Ezekiel will be sent to tell them that the city will fall.

the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the Chebar canal, and the hand of the LORD was upon him there.

Three things came to him: visions, the word, and the hand of the LORD. Seeing, hearing, and being gripped. Ezekiel is a priest by birth, but his real work will be as a prophet. And he will be a priest-like prophet: a book full of holiness, glory, the temple and the question of how a holy God can live among an unclean people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A storm comes out of the north — cloud, brightness, flashing fire, and in the fire something like gleaming metal (v. 4). Out of it come four living creatures with a human likeness, four faces and four wings (vv. 5-6), legs straight and feet shining like bronze, human hands under their wings (vv. 7-8). Each has the face of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle (v. 10). They move straight ahead wherever the spirit goes (vv. 9, 12), and they look like burning coals and torches, darting like lightning (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The living creatures show a God of overwhelming majesty, whose servants move only at his Spirit's direction.

verseByVerse.quote: As I looked, behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually, and in the midst of the fire, as it were gleaming metal. And from the midst of it came the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance: they had a human likeness, but each had four faces, and each of them had four wings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I looked, behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually, and in the midst of the fire, as it were gleaming metal.

Storm, cloud, fire, brightness — these are the signs that went with God's appearing at Sinai, where there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and the LORD had descended on it in fire (Exod 19:16, 18). The ESV notes that gleaming metal may be "amber": something glowing at the heart of the fire.

Notice how Ezekiel describes it. Over and over in this chapter he says as it were, likeness, appearance. He is straining for words. What he saw was real, but it was beyond ordinary language, so he can only say what it was like.

And from the midst of it came the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance: they had a human likeness,

but each had four faces, and each of them had four wings.

Later Ezekiel will see the same beings again and say, I knew that they were cherubim (10:20). Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life (Gen 3:24), and their golden images spread their wings over the ark in the Most Holy Place, where God said There I will meet with you (Exod 25:22). Israel praised God as the one enthroned upon the cherubim (Ps 80:1).

So the vision is saying: the throne that belonged in the Most Holy Place in Jerusalem has come to Babylon. God's presence has not been captured in a building. It moves.

verseByVerse.quote: Their legs were straight, and the soles of their feet were like the sole of a calf's foot. And they sparkled like burnished bronze. Under their wings on their four sides they had human hands. And the four had their faces and their wings thus: their wings touched one another. Each one of them went straight forward, without turning as they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their legs were straight, and the soles of their feet were like the sole of a calf's foot. And they sparkled like burnished bronze.

Under their wings on their four sides they had human hands. And the four had their faces and their wings thus:

their wings touched one another. Each one of them went straight forward, without turning as they went.

Straight legs, feet like a calf's, shining like polished bronze; hands for work under the wings; wings touching one another so that the four form a single moving square. And they go straight forward, without turning.

That last detail comes back again and again (vv. 9, 12, 17). The servants of God do not waver, hesitate, or turn aside. They face every direction at once, so they never need to turn round. There is a picture here of what God's service looks like: single-minded, whole-hearted, going where he sends without looking back. No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God, Jesus said (Luke 9:62).

verseByVerse.quote: As for the likeness of their faces, each had a human face. The four had the face of a lion on the right side, the four had the face of an ox on the left side, and the four had the face of an eagle. Such were their faces. And their wings were spread out above. Each creature had two wings, each of which touched the wing of another, while two covered their bodies. And each went straight forward. Wherever the spirit would go, they went, without turning as they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the likeness of their faces, each had a human face. The four had the face of a lion on the right side, the four had the face of an ox on the left side, and the four had the face of an eagle.

A man, a lion, an ox, an eagle. Each is the chief of its kind: humanity, the wild beasts, the domestic animals, the birds. Together they suggest that all the strength, wisdom and swiftness of creation are gathered around God's throne in his service.

John saw the same four around the throne in heaven: the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight, and day and night they never cease to say, "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty" (Rev 4:7-8). The creatures Ezekiel saw in the storm are worshippers. Everything in creation that is greatest exists to adore God.

Such were their faces. And their wings were spread out above. Each creature had two wings, each of which touched the wing of another, while two covered their bodies.

Two wings stretched out to one another; two wings covering themselves. Even these mighty beings cover themselves before God — as the seraphim in Isaiah's vision covered their faces and feet (Isa 6:2).

And each went straight forward. Wherever the spirit would go, they went, without turning as they went.

The ESV notes that spirit may be rendered "Spirit". The creatures have no agenda of their own. Wherever the spirit would go, they went. Their perfect freedom is perfect obedience.

That is the pattern for every believer. Jesus said The wind blows where it wishes... So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit (John 3:8). A life led by God's Spirit is not aimless; it goes straight, wherever he leads.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of torches moving to and fro among the living creatures. And the fire was bright, and out of the fire went forth lightning. And the living creatures darted to and fro, like the appearance of a flash of lightning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of torches moving to and fro among the living creatures. And the fire was bright, and out of the fire went forth lightning.

And the living creatures darted to and fro, like the appearance of a flash of lightning.

Coals, torches, lightning. The whole vision is alive with fire and speed. This is not a calm, domesticated God.

Fire in Scripture speaks of God's holiness — his purity that burns up what is unclean. Our God is a consuming fire (Heb 12:29). Ezekiel is about to be sent to a people who have treated God lightly. Before he says a word to them, he must see that the God they have despised is fire.

The church in every age needs this vision. We are always in danger of thinking of God as a comfortable helper who fits into our plans. The God of Ezekiel 1 is utterly beyond our control, and he is coming in the storm.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Beside each creature is a wheel gleaming like beryl, built as it were a wheel within a wheel (vv. 15-16), able to go in any direction without turning (v. 17). Their rims are tall, awesome and full of eyes all around (v. 18). The wheels move and rise with the creatures, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: God's throne is not fixed to one place; it goes anywhere, and it sees everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as I looked at the living creatures, I saw a wheel on the earth beside the living creatures, one for each of the four of them. As for the appearance of the wheels and their construction: their appearance was like the gleaming of beryl. And the four had the same likeness, their appearance and construction being as it were a wheel within a wheel. When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went. And their rims were tall and awesome, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now as I looked at the living creatures, I saw a wheel on the earth beside the living creatures, one for each of the four of them.

As for the appearance of the wheels and their construction: their appearance was like the gleaming of beryl. And the four had the same likeness, their appearance and construction being as it were a wheel within a wheel.

Wheels mean movement. Beside the creatures are wheels that gleam like precious stone, each built as it were a wheel within a wheel — perhaps two wheels set crosswise, so that they can roll in any direction.

When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went.

The whole throne is mobile. The people in Jerusalem believed God lived in their temple and would never leave it. The exiles in Babylon feared that God had been left behind in Jerusalem. The wheels answer both errors. God's throne is not stuck in one place. It can go anywhere — to judge a city that trusts in its temple, and to meet exiles by a canal.

Solomon had already said it at the temple's dedication: heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built! (1 Kgs 8:27).

And their rims were tall and awesome, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.

Wheels full of eyes all around. Nothing escapes this God. The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good (Prov 15:3).

That is a warning to the people in Jerusalem who thought no one saw what they did in secret (8:12). And it is a comfort to the exiles, who feared they had dropped out of God's sight. The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chr 16:9). The same eyes that expose sin watch over the faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them; and when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose. Wherever the spirit wanted to go, they went, and the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels. When those went, these went; and when those stood, these stood; and when those rose from the earth, the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them; and when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose.

Wherever the spirit wanted to go, they went, and the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

When those went, these went; and when those stood, these stood; and when those rose from the earth, the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

Ezekiel repeats himself, as if the sight is too big to take in: when they went, these went; when they stood, these stood; when they rose, these rose. Everything moves together, in perfect harmony, because one spirit drives it all. The ESV notes that the spirit of the living creatures may also be read "the spirit of life".

There is no friction in God's government. The creatures, the wheels and the Spirit never pull against each other. What God wills is done, completely and at once.

That is a great comfort in a world that looks chaotic. To the exiles, history seemed to be spinning out of control — Babylon rising, Judah collapsing. But over the storm is a throne, and the wheels of history go only where the Spirit of God sends them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–28 — The Likeness of the Glory of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Above the creatures is an expanse shining like crystal (v. 22); their wings sound like many waters, like the voice of the Almighty (v. 24), and a voice comes from above (v. 25). Above the expanse is a throne like sapphire, and on the throne a likeness with a human appearance (v. 26), glowing like fire and surrounded by brightness like a rainbow (vv. 27-28). Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Ezekiel's ministry begins where all true ministry begins: face down before the glory of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Over the heads of the living creatures there was the likeness of an expanse, shining like awe-inspiring crystal, spread out above their heads. And under the expanse their wings were stretched out straight, one toward another. And each creature had two wings covering its body. And when they went, I heard the sound of their wings like the sound of many waters, like the sound of the Almighty, a sound of tumult like the sound of an army. When they stood still, they let down their wings. And there came a voice from above the expanse over their heads. When they stood still, they let down their wings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over the heads of the living creatures there was the likeness of an expanse, shining like awe-inspiring crystal, spread out above their heads.

Now Ezekiel's eyes move upward. Above the creatures is a platform, shining like crystal. It separates the creatures below from what is above. When Moses and the elders saw God at Sinai, There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness (Exod 24:10).

And under the expanse their wings were stretched out straight, one toward another. And each creature had two wings covering its body.

And when they went, I heard the sound of their wings like the sound of many waters, like the sound of the Almighty, a sound of tumult like the sound of an army. When they stood still, they let down their wings.

Now sound joins sight. The wings roar like the sound of many waters — a waterfall, the ocean — like the sound of the Almighty, like an army on the move. When John saw the risen Christ, his voice was like the roar of many waters (Rev 1:15).

And there came a voice from above the expanse over their heads. When they stood still, they let down their wings.

Then everything stops. The wings drop. And a voice comes from above. The whole spectacle — storm, fire, creatures, wheels — falls silent so that God can speak. The vision exists for the voice. It is the same in our worship: all the glory of God is meant to bring us to silence before his word.

verseByVerse.quote: And above the expanse over their heads there was the likeness of a throne, in appearance like sapphire; and seated above the likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance. And upward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were gleaming metal, like the appearance of fire enclosed all around. And downward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and there was brightness around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And above the expanse over their heads there was the likeness of a throne, in appearance like sapphire; and seated above the likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance.

Here is the heart of the vision. Above everything, a throne, blue like sapphire — the ESV notes it may be "lapis lazuli". And on the throne, a likeness with a human appearance.

Ezekiel is careful. He does not say he saw God's face; man shall not see me and live (Exod 33:20). He saw a likeness with a human appearance. Yet it is astonishing that the form on the throne of the universe looked like a man.

The New Testament explains why. No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known (John 1:18). John says Isaiah, who saw the Lord on his throne, saw his glory and spoke of him — that is, of Jesus (John 12:41). The glory of God has a human face, because the eternal Son took our nature: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). Ezekiel saw a likeness. We know the name.

And upward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were gleaming metal, like the appearance of fire enclosed all around. And downward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and there was brightness around him.

Fire above, fire below, brightness all around. The figure on the throne is human in form and blazing with divine glory. John's vision of the risen Jesus is strikingly similar: His eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace and his face was like the sun shining in full strength (Rev 1:14-16). The man on the throne is not less than God.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking.

Around the throne, a rainbow. After the flood God said, I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant, and When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant (Gen 9:13, 16). John saw it too: around the throne was a rainbow (Rev 4:3).

This matters enormously. Ezekiel has just seen a storm of holiness coming out of the north. He is about to be sent to announce judgment on Jerusalem. And the throne of that judgment is ringed with the sign of God's covenant mercy. Judgment is real, but it is judgment from a God who remembers his promises. The storm does not have the last word; the rainbow does.

Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. Notice the layers of caution: the appearance, of the likeness, of the glory. Ezekiel has not seen God as he is in himself. He has seen the glory, and even that only in likeness. And yet it is enough to put him flat on the ground.

I fell on my face. That is the only right response. Isaiah said Woe is me! For I am lost (Isa 6:5). John fell at his feet as though dead (Rev 1:17). Saul of Tarsus, blinded by a light from heaven, fell to the ground (Acts 9:3-4).

Here is a test for our own knowledge of God: has it ever put us on our faces? A God who never humbles us is not the God of Ezekiel 1. But notice what follows: I heard the voice of one speaking. God did not show Ezekiel his glory to crush him, but to speak to him. The next words will be stand on your feet (2:1). The glory that throws us down is the glory that raises us up and sends us out.

This glory will be the thread through the whole book. Ezekiel will watch it leave the temple and stand on the mountain east of Jerusalem (11:22-23), and he will watch it come back: the glory of the LORD filled the temple (43:5). The book ends with a city whose name is The LORD Is There (48:35). Christians know where that glory came to live: the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6).

1.title: Visions of God by the Chebar Canal
1.overview:
In the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's exile, Ezekiel the priest was among the exiles by the Chebar canal in Babylon when the heavens were opened and he saw visions of God. The word of the LORD came to him, and the hand of the LORD was upon him (vv. 1-3).

A storm came out of the north, full of cloud and fire, and in it four living creatures, each with four faces — man, lion, ox and eagle — and four wings. They shone like bronze and burning coals, darted like lightning, and went straight forward wherever the spirit went (vv. 4-14).

Beside each creature was a gleaming wheel, like a wheel within a wheel, able to move in any direction, its rims full of eyes. The wheels moved and rose with the creatures, because the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels (vv. 15-21).

Above them was a shining expanse, and the sound of their wings was like many waters and like the voice of the Almighty. When they stood still, a voice came from above. Above the expanse was a throne like sapphire, and on it a likeness with a human appearance, blazing with fire and surrounded by brightness like a rainbow. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD, and Ezekiel fell on his face and heard a voice speaking (vv. 22-28).
1.theology:
God is not confined to a place. He opens heaven over his people in exile, and his throne moves wherever his Spirit wills (vv. 1, 15-21; 1 Kgs 8:27; Ps 139:7-10).

God is holy fire and overwhelming majesty; the mightiest creatures cover themselves before him and exist to worship him (vv. 4, 11, 13-14; Rev 4:6-8; Heb 12:29).

God sees everything, to expose the wicked and to support the faithful (v. 18; Prov 15:3; 2 Chr 16:9).

God's government of history is perfectly harmonious: everything moves where his Spirit sends it (vv. 12, 19-21).

The throne of judgment is surrounded by the sign of covenant mercy (v. 28; Gen 9:13-16; Rev 4:3).

The glory on the throne appeared in human likeness, pointing to the incarnate Son, in whom the glory of God is fully seen (vv. 26-28; John 1:14, 18; 12:41; 2 Cor 4:6; Heb 1:3; Rev 1:13-17).

True knowledge of God humbles before it sends: the prophet falls on his face and hears the voice (v. 28; Isa 6:5).
1.examples:
A priest's thirtieth birthday spent by a canal in Babylon.

The heavens opened over a refugee settlement.

A throne on wheels.

Faces turned every way, so they never have to turn back.

Eyes on every rim.

Wings like a waterfall, falling silent for a voice.

A man on the throne of the universe.

A rainbow around the storm.

Face down, and then: stand on your feet.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you."<sup>2</sup>And as he spoke to me, the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me.<sup>3</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, I send you to the people of Israel, to nations of rebels, who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me to this very day.<sup>4</sup>The descendants also are impudent and stubborn: I send you to them, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.'<sup>5</sup>And whether they hear or refuse to hear (for they are a rebellious house) they will know that a prophet has been among them.<sup>6</sup>And you, son of man, be not afraid of them, nor be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with you and you sit on scorpions. Be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house.<sup>7</sup>And you shall speak my words to them, whether they hear or refuse to hear, for they are a rebellious house.<sup>8</sup>"But you, son of man, hear what I say to you. Be not rebellious like that rebellious house; open your mouth and eat what I give you."<sup>9</sup>And when I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me, and behold, a scroll of a book was in it.<sup>10</sup>And he spread it before me. And it had writing on the front and on the back, and there were written on it words of lamentation and mourning and woe.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The voice from the throne says Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you, and the Spirit enters Ezekiel and sets him on his feet (vv. 1-2). He is sent to nations of rebels, a people impudent and stubborn like their fathers, to say Thus says the Lord GOD (vv. 3-4). Whether they hear or refuse to hear, they will know a prophet has been among them (v. 5). He must not fear them, though it is like sitting among thorns and scorpions (v. 6); he must simply speak God's words (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's success is measured by faithfulness to God's word, not by the response of his hearers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you." And as he spoke to me, the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, "Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you."

Ezekiel is face down before the glory (1:28). The first words he hears are a name and a command.

The name is Son of man, and God will call him that more than ninety times in this book. The ESV notes that it may be rendered "Son of Adam". It means simply: human being, mortal, made of dust. The psalm asks, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him? (Ps 8:4). Set beside the blazing figure on the throne, Ezekiel is reminded what he is — a creature.

That is not an insult. It is the ground of his ministry. God does not send angels to rebels; he sends a man, one of their own, weak and mortal, to carry his word.

Jesus often called himself the Son of Man. He drew chiefly on Daniel's vision of one like a son of man who comes with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom (Dan 7:13-14). But he also took up all the lowliness of the name: the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt 8:20), and came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Ezekiel was a son of man sent to rebels. Jesus is the Son of Man who came to die for them.

And as he spoke to me, the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me.

God commands, stand on your feet — and then does it for him. The Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet. What God requires, God supplies.

Every servant of God lives by this. We are commanded to stand, to speak, to obey, and we cannot do it in our own strength. Our sufficiency is from God, who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit (2 Cor 3:5-6).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, I send you to the people of Israel, to nations of rebels, who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me to this very day. The descendants also are impudent and stubborn: I send you to them, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.' And whether they hear or refuse to hear (for they are a rebellious house) they will know that a prophet has been among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, "Son of man, I send you to the people of Israel, to nations of rebels, who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me to this very day.

Listen to the words: rebels, rebelled, transgressed. God's own people are described as nations of rebels, as if they were no different from the pagan nations around them. And it is not new; They and their fathers have done it to this very day.

The descendants also are impudent and stubborn: I send you to them, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.'

Impudent and stubborn. And yet: I send you to them. God keeps sending messengers to people who have rejected every messenger before. That is patience beyond anything human.

Ezekiel's message has one foundation: Thus says the Lord GOD. Not his opinions, not his insights. The authority of the preacher is entirely borrowed. That is both humbling and freeing. He does not have to be clever; he has to be faithful.

And whether they hear or refuse to hear (for they are a rebellious house) they will know that a prophet has been among them.

Here is the measure of success God gives him: not whether they hear, but that they will know that a prophet has been among them. The result is in God's hands. The task is in Ezekiel's.

That is a liberating word for every pastor, missionary, parent or friend who has spoken the truth and seen no response. You are not responsible for the hearing. You are responsible for the speaking. And one day, God says, When this comes—and come it will!— then they will know that a prophet has been among them (33:33).

Jesus lived this. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). He was not a failure. He was faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, son of man, be not afraid of them, nor be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with you and you sit on scorpions. Be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house. And you shall speak my words to them, whether they hear or refuse to hear, for they are a rebellious house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, son of man, be not afraid of them, nor be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with you and you sit on scorpions. Be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house.

Three times: be not afraid. God knows his servant will be tempted to fear — fear of what people say, fear of how they look at you. Ministry among the hostile is like sitting in a thorn bush on top of scorpions. (The ESV notes that the last phrase may be "on scorpion plants" — prickly desert plants. Either way, it hurts.)

God does not promise that it won't hurt. He commands him not to be ruled by fear. The fear of people is broken by the fear of God, and Ezekiel has just been on his face before the throne. Once you have seen that glory, the frowns of rebels shrink.

And you shall speak my words to them, whether they hear or refuse to hear, for they are a rebellious house.

My words. The same phrase again: whether they hear or refuse to hear. It is the refrain of Ezekiel's commission. Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season (2 Tim 4:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — A Scroll of Lamentation and Mourning and Woe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before he speaks to rebels, Ezekiel is warned: Be not rebellious like that rebellious house; open your mouth and eat what I give you (v. 8). A hand holds out a scroll (v. 9), written on the front and on the back with words of lamentation and mourning and woe (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The messenger must first receive and submit to the word he is sent to deliver.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you, son of man, hear what I say to you. Be not rebellious like that rebellious house; open your mouth and eat what I give you." And when I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me, and behold, a scroll of a book was in it. And he spread it before me. And it had writing on the front and on the back, and there were written on it words of lamentation and mourning and woe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But you, son of man, hear what I say to you. Be not rebellious like that rebellious house; open your mouth and eat what I give you."

Now the warning turns on Ezekiel himself: Be not rebellious like that rebellious house. The greatest danger to a preacher of repentance is not the hardness of his hearers but his own. Before he speaks the word, he must obey it.

And the first test of obedience is strange: open your mouth and eat what I give you. He must take God's word into himself before he gives it out. We who teach will be judged with greater strictness (Jas 3:1).

And when I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me, and behold, a scroll of a book was in it.

And he spread it before me. And it had writing on the front and on the back, and there were written on it words of lamentation and mourning and woe.

Scrolls were normally written on one side only. This one is full on both sides — no room to add anything. The message is complete, and it is God's, not Ezekiel's. John saw a scroll like it in the hand of the one on the throne, written within and on the back (Rev 5:1).

And the content: lamentation and mourning and woe. Ezekiel's first years of ministry will be almost entirely bad news. He is not sent to tell people what they want to hear. But the book that begins with woe will end with a new heart, dry bones living, a river of life and a city called The LORD Is There (48:35). The woe is not the last word, but it has to be spoken first.

2.title: Son of Man, I Send You
2.overview:
The voice from the throne calls Ezekiel Son of man and tells him to stand, and the Spirit enters him and sets him on his feet. God sends him to the people of Israel, a nation of rebels, impudent and stubborn like their fathers, to say Thus says the Lord GOD. Whether they hear or refuse to hear, they will know that a prophet has been among them. He must not be afraid of their words or their looks, though it will be like sitting among thorns and scorpions; he must speak God's words (vv. 1-7).

Ezekiel himself must not be rebellious. He is told to open his mouth and eat what God gives him, and a hand holds out a scroll written on both sides with words of lamentation, mourning and woe (vv. 8-10).
2.theology:
God's messenger is a mortal, a son of man, enabled by the Spirit to stand and speak (vv. 1-2; Ps 8:4; 2 Cor 3:5-6). Jesus took the title in both its lowliness and its glory (Mark 10:45; Dan 7:13-14).

God keeps sending his word to a rebellious people; the preacher's authority is wholly borrowed: Thus says the Lord GOD (vv. 3-4).

Faithfulness, not response, is the measure of a messenger (vv. 5, 7; 33:33; John 1:11).

The fear of people is overcome by the fear of God (v. 6).

The messenger must receive and obey the word before he delivers it (vv. 8-10; Jas 3:1).
2.examples:
A name that means: you are made of dust.

A command to stand, and the Spirit who stands you up.

Success measured without counting converts.

Sitting in a thorn bush on a nest of scorpions.

A scroll with no room left to write your own opinions.

He who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey (v. 3). He is sent not to foreigners who cannot understand him — they would listen — but to Israel, who will not listen because they will not listen to God (vv. 4-7). So God makes Ezekiel's forehead Like emery harder than flint (vv. 8-9), and tells him to take all God's words into his heart and speak them to the exiles, whether they hear or refuse to hear (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: God's word is sweet to the one who receives it, and God hardens his servant to stand against hardened hearers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, eat whatever you find here. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel." So I opened my mouth, and he gave me this scroll to eat. And he said to me, "Son of man, feed your belly with this scroll that I give you and fill your stomach with it." Then I ate it, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, "Son of man, eat whatever you find here. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel."

So I opened my mouth, and he gave me this scroll to eat.

Notice the order: eat, then go, then speak. Ezekiel does not take the scroll and read it aloud. He has to take it in. The word must become part of him before it comes out of him.

And notice who feeds whom: he gave me this scroll to eat. Ezekiel opens his mouth; God puts the word in it. The preacher is first of all a receiver.

And he said to me, "Son of man, feed your belly with this scroll that I give you and fill your stomach with it." Then I ate it, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey.

Feed your belly... fill your stomach. Not a taste but a meal. Man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt 4:4).

And the surprise: a scroll full of lamentation and mourning and woe (2:10) tastes as sweet as honey. How can woe be sweet? Because it is God's word, and whatever God says is good to the one who loves him. How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! (Ps 119:103). Jeremiah said the same (Jer 15:16).

John was given a scroll to eat too: It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter (Rev 10:10). Both things are true of every faithful messenger. The word is sweet because it is God's; it becomes bitter as he carries it to people who will not hear. Ezekiel will feel the bitterness by verse 14.

Here is a question for our own Bible reading: do we find God's word sweet only when it comforts us? The prophet found it sweet when it was full of woe.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, go to the house of Israel and speak with my words to them. For you are not sent to a people of foreign speech and a hard language, but to the house of Israel— not to many peoples of foreign speech and a hard language, whose words you cannot understand. Surely, if I sent you to such, they would listen to you. But the house of Israel will not be willing to listen to you, for they are not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, "Son of man, go to the house of Israel and speak with my words to them.

For you are not sent to a people of foreign speech and a hard language, but to the house of Israel—

not to many peoples of foreign speech and a hard language, whose words you cannot understand. Surely, if I sent you to such, they would listen to you.

Ezekiel has no language barrier. He speaks the same language as his hearers, shares their history, their Scriptures, their exile. And God says that is exactly the problem. If he were sent to foreigners, they would listen to you.

That came true again and again. Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching. Jesus said if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago (Matt 11:21), and Paul told the Jews of Rome, this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen (Acts 28:28).

Familiarity is one of the great dangers to people who have grown up with God's word. They have heard it all. It no longer surprises them. Outsiders sometimes hear with fresher ears than insiders.

But the house of Israel will not be willing to listen to you, for they are not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart.

They are not willing to listen to me. Ezekiel must not take their rejection personally. It is not about his eloquence. They are rejecting God. Jesus said the same to his disciples: The one who rejects you rejects me (Luke 10:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have made your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads. Like emery harder than flint have I made your forehead. Fear them not, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house." Moreover, he said to me, "Son of man, all my words that I shall speak to you receive in your heart, and hear with your ears. And go to the exiles, to your people, and speak to them and say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD,' whether they hear or refuse to hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I have made your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads.

Like emery harder than flint have I made your forehead. Fear them not, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house."

They have hard foreheads; God gives Ezekiel a harder one — Like emery harder than flint. It is a picture of stubbornness turned to good use: a holy determination that will not be worn down by their resistance.

This is not harshness of heart. Ezekiel will sit overwhelmed among these people (v. 15). It is firmness of face — the refusal to be moved from God's word by pressure. The Servant of the LORD said I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame (Isa 50:7), and Jesus, knowing what waited for him, set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51).

Moreover, he said to me, "Son of man, all my words that I shall speak to you receive in your heart, and hear with your ears.

And go to the exiles, to your people, and speak to them and say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD,' whether they hear or refuse to hear."

Receive in your heart before hear with your ears — the heart first. And then: to your people. They are rebels, but they are his people. God does not let his prophet speak about them as outsiders. A preacher who does not love the people he warns will not warn them well.

And notice the word all: all my words that I shall speak to you. Ezekiel is not free to choose the parts of the message that will go down well and leave out the rest. God had told Israel long before, You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it (Deut 4:2). A preacher who edits God's word to suit his hearers has stopped being a watchman.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–15 — Overwhelmed Among Them Seven Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel up to the roar of the living creatures and the cry Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place! (vv. 12-13). He goes in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, with the hand of the LORD strong on him (v. 14), and comes to the exiles at Tel-abib, where he sits among them overwhelmed for seven days (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The messenger must first sit where his hearers sit and feel the weight of the word he carries.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great earthquake: "Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place!" It was the sound of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another, and the sound of the wheels beside them, and the sound of a great earthquake. The Spirit lifted me up and took me away, and I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the LORD being strong upon me. And I came to the exiles at Tel-abib, who were dwelling by the Chebar canal, and I sat where they were dwelling. And I sat there overwhelmed among them seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great earthquake: "Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place!"

It was the sound of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another, and the sound of the wheels beside them, and the sound of a great earthquake.

As Ezekiel is carried away, he hears the vision rumbling behind him, and a cry of praise: Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place! (The ESV notes that Spirit may be "wind", and voice may be "sound".) The glory is leaving the place of vision, but it is blessed wherever it goes.

The Spirit lifted me up and took me away, and I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the LORD being strong upon me.

The honey has turned bitter. Ezekiel goes in bitterness in the heat of my spirit. That is honest. He has seen the glory, he has eaten the sweet word, and now he is walking toward a hard people with a hard message, and he does not feel good about it.

But the hand of the LORD being strong upon me. Faithful ministry is often done not because the servant feels like it, but because God's hand will not let him go. Necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! (1 Cor 9:16).

And I came to the exiles at Tel-abib, who were dwelling by the Chebar canal, and I sat where they were dwelling. And I sat there overwhelmed among them seven days.

Ezekiel does not arrive and start preaching. I sat where they were dwelling. For seven days he says nothing, overwhelmed. Job's friends did the same, and it was the best thing they did: they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him (Job 2:13).

There is deep wisdom here for anyone who must bring God's word to suffering people. Sit where they sit first. Feel what they feel. Let the weight of their situation and the weight of God's message overwhelm you before you open your mouth. Christ did more than sit where we sit; he became one of us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Watchman for the House of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After seven days God says Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel (vv. 16-17). If he fails to warn the wicked, the wicked will die, but God will require his blood at Ezekiel's hand; if he warns them and they refuse, he has delivered his soul (vv. 18-19). The same holds for a righteous person who turns to sin: warned, he may live; unwarned, his blood is required of the watchman (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Those entrusted with God's word are accountable for warning others, while each hearer is accountable for his response.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of seven days, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me. If I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, in order to save his life, that wicked person shall die for his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness, or from his wicked way, he shall die for his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And at the end of seven days, the word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me.

A watchman stood on the city wall, looking out for danger. If he saw an enemy coming, he blew the trumpet. His job was not to fight the enemy or to save the city by himself, but to warn.

And the danger Ezekiel watches for is not Babylon. It is God himself, coming in judgment. The warning is from me. God warns people about God. That is mercy: the Judge sends a herald before the judgment, so that people can turn.

If I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, in order to save his life, that wicked person shall die for his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand.

But if you warn the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness, or from his wicked way, he shall die for his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul.

Two cases. In both, the wicked person who does not turn dies for his iniquity (the ESV notes it may be "in his iniquity"). He is responsible for his own sin. But the watchman is responsible too. If he stays silent, his blood I will require at your hand.

This is a sobering word for everyone God has entrusted with his truth — pastors most of all, but also parents, teachers and every Christian who knows the gospel. Silence is not neutral. Paul could say to the Ephesian elders, I am innocent of the blood of all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:26-27). Could we say it?

You will have delivered your soul. The watchman's own standing before God is bound up with his faithfulness. Paul told a young pastor, Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers (1 Tim 4:16). The one who warns others must keep watch over his own soul first.

And notice the purpose: in order to save his life. The warning is not an accusation for its own sake. It is a rescue attempt. Christian preaching warns because it loves: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone (Col 1:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, if a righteous person turns from his righteousness and commits injustice, and I lay a stumbling block before him, he shall die. Because you have not warned him, he shall die for his sin, and his righteous deeds that he has done shall not be remembered, but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the righteous person not to sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because he took warning, and you will have delivered your soul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again, if a righteous person turns from his righteousness and commits injustice, and I lay a stumbling block before him, he shall die. Because you have not warned him, he shall die for his sin, and his righteous deeds that he has done shall not be remembered, but his blood I will require at your hand.

The second case is the person who has been living rightly and turns away. God will lay a stumbling block — let him fall under the consequences of his choice. And past righteousness is no insurance: his righteous deeds that he has done shall not be remembered.

Does this mean a true believer can be lost? Ezekiel is speaking of outward covenant life in Israel, and the New Testament holds two truths together. Those who truly belong to Christ will be kept: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). And those who fall away show that they were never truly his: They went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). But the way God keeps his people is through warnings like this one. Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart... exhort one another every day (Heb 3:12-13). The warning is one of the means by which God preserves.

But if you warn the righteous person not to sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because he took warning, and you will have delivered your soul."

And here is the happy case: a warning given, taken, and a life saved. Believers need warning too, not only unbelievers. A loving church tells its members the truth before they fall. Leaders are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account (Heb 13:17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the valley Ezekiel sees the glory again and falls on his face; the Spirit sets him on his feet (vv. 22-24). He is told to shut himself in his house, bound with cords (vv. 24-25), and God makes his tongue cling to the roof of his mouth so that he cannot reprove them (v. 26). But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and he will say Thus says the Lord GOD (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet speaks only when God speaks; his silence and his words alike belong to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the hand of the LORD was upon me there. And he said to me, "Arise, go out into the valley, and there I will speak with you." So I arose and went out into the valley, and behold, the glory of the LORD stood there, like the glory that I had seen by the Chebar canal, and I fell on my face. But the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and he spoke with me and said to me, "Go, shut yourself within your house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the hand of the LORD was upon me there. And he said to me, "Arise, go out into the valley, and there I will speak with you."

So I arose and went out into the valley, and behold, the glory of the LORD stood there, like the glory that I had seen by the Chebar canal, and I fell on my face.

The ESV notes that valley may be "plain". Ezekiel goes out alone, and the glory is waiting for him. The pattern of chapter 1 repeats: glory, and the prophet on his face. He will need to see it again and again. No servant of God can live on one vision.

But the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and he spoke with me and said to me, "Go, shut yourself within your house.

And again the Spirit sets him on his feet (2:2). But this time the command is unexpected: not "go and preach" but shut yourself within your house.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, O son of man, behold, cords will be placed upon you, and you shall be bound with them, so that you cannot go out among the people. And I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, so that you shall be mute and unable to reprove them, for they are a rebellious house. But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.' He who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, O son of man, behold, cords will be placed upon you, and you shall be bound with them, so that you cannot go out among the people.

And I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, so that you shall be mute and unable to reprove them, for they are a rebellious house.

A prophet who is bound and cannot speak. It is a sign in itself: God's word is being withdrawn from a people who would not hear it. Ezekiel's ordinary speech is taken from him, so that he cannot even argue with them.

Who places the cords? The verse does not say. It may be the exiles themselves, hostile to a prophet they do not want to hear, or it may be a restraint God puts on him as part of the sign. Either way, the point is the same: even the opposition of his hearers is inside God's plan for his servant. Nothing done to Ezekiel escapes the hand of the LORD that is on him.

This muteness lasts a long time. It ends only on the day news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen: my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute (33:22; 24:27).

But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.' He who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house.

So how does Ezekiel prophesy all through chapters 4-32? Because when I speak with you, I will open your mouth. He is silent except when God gives him a word. Everything that comes out of his mouth in those years is Thus says the Lord GOD.

That is a searching standard. How much of what we say about God is really his word, and how much is our own talk? Ezekiel's mouth was shut to everything but the message.

He who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse. Jesus ended his parables the same way: He who has ears, let him hear (Matt 13:9). The word is spoken; the responsibility now rests with the hearer.

3.title: A Watchman for the House of Israel
3.overview:
Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it is sweet as honey. God sends him not to foreigners, who would listen, but to the house of Israel, who will not listen because they will not listen to God. He makes Ezekiel's forehead harder than flint and tells him to receive God's words in his heart and speak them to the exiles, whether they hear or refuse to hear (vv. 1-11).

The Spirit lifts him up to the sound of the living creatures and the cry, Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place. He goes in bitterness with the hand of the LORD strong on him, and sits overwhelmed among the exiles at Tel-abib for seven days (vv. 12-15).

Then God makes him a watchman for the house of Israel. If he fails to warn the wicked or the righteous who turns to sin, they will die in their sin and God will require their blood at his hand; if he warns them, he has delivered his soul, and those who take warning will live (vv. 16-21).

In the valley he sees the glory again and falls on his face. The Spirit sets him on his feet and tells him to shut himself in his house, bound, with his tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth, unable to reprove them — except when God speaks and opens his mouth to say, Thus says the Lord GOD (vv. 22-27).
3.theology:
God's word must be received inwardly before it is spoken outwardly, and it is sweet even when its content is woe (vv. 1-3, 10; Ps 119:103; Rev 10:9-10).

Rejection of God's messenger is rejection of God; familiarity can harden people more than foreignness (vv. 5-7; Matt 11:21; Acts 28:28).

God strengthens his servants with holy firmness against hard hearts (vv. 8-9; Isa 50:7; Luke 9:51).

The messenger must sit where his hearers sit (v. 15; Job 2:13).

Those entrusted with God's word are accountable to warn; each hearer is accountable for his response (vv. 17-21; Acts 20:26-27; Heb 13:17). Warnings to the righteous are one of the means by which God keeps his people (v. 21; Heb 3:12-14; John 10:28; 1 John 2:19).

The prophet speaks only when God speaks (vv. 26-27).
3.examples:
A scroll full of woe that tastes like honey.

A people who share your language and still cannot hear you.

A forehead harder than flint, and a heart that sits overwhelmed.

Seven days of silence before one word.

A watchman whose silence has blood on it.

A mouth shut to everything except Thus says the Lord GOD.
